item.title: Anthropic's bill makes it nearly impossible to halt dangerous AI training
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-eightythousand-anthropic的法案让人几乎没法叫停危险的ai训练/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-eightythousand-anthropic的法案让人几乎没法叫停危险的ai训练/
item.description: The bill compresses the power to halt training into a single Commerce Secretary signature and a single DC court decision within 45 days—when models actually cause harm, there's almost no time to hit the brakes.
item.content:encoded:
The bill compresses the power to halt training into a single Commerce Secretary signature and a single DC court decision within 45 days—when models actually cause harm, there's almost no time to hit the brakes.

A dense solo episode: the evidence chains and perspectives on three major scandals are laid out clearly and worth hearing in full.

1:34 Bill compresses authority to stop dangerous training through a dangerously narrow bottleneck
Under the federal AI bill that Anthropic privately championed, the only way to halt a model's training is for the Commerce Secretary to personally sign off and submit the case to a single federal court in Washington DC. The government must prove the risk is ‘imminent’, must prove lighter interventions won't work, and judges must review from scratch without deference to regulators. Any halt order expires automatically after 45 days; reauthorizing requires proving the case all over again. More critically, even whether ‘a 10% human extinction probability within the next year’counts as ‘imminent’ is undefined—and that gap determines whether this gate can actually block truly catastrophic risks.

4:02 CEO estimates 25% disaster probability, yet company strips halt authority
The contradiction: this bill comes from a company whose CEO publicly puts the probability of AI ‘causing major chaos’at 25% and has written that ‘recursive self-improvement must proceed with extreme care, if at all’. The host sees why—Anthropic has been in frequent conflict with the Trump administration this year and fears federal discretionary power will be weaponized for political concessions rather than genuinely controlling dangerous research. But he argues the solution shouldn't be stripping away state power too; instead preserve states like California's independent halt authority, or at least let state attorneys general petition the DC court as well. You shouldn't stake everything on one agency's review by a single court.

5:15 Bill would retroactively eliminate state-level AI safety laws nationwide
The bill not only narrows federal authority but also bars states from requiring AI companies to disclose safety plans, undergo independent audits, or report incidents—effectively retroactively nullifying flagship AI laws already passed in California, Illinois, and New York. There's a subtler provision: states had the power to halt models presenting ‘major catastrophic risk’using ‘statute, regulation, directive, court decision or other action’; under the bill's design, that power eventually disappears too. The result: even if California's government unanimously determined an unreleased model could kill everyone in the state, it would have no power to legislate or seek a court injunction—only hope the Commerce Secretary will run that process.

8:58 OpenAI fired three safety researchers on the same afternoon over disputed evidence
Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang were each fired at a 2 p.m. meeting on the same afternoon, with contradictory and unpersuasive justifications. OpenAI later claimed the real reason was ‘broken trust’but refused to explain. According to reports, the trigger was a leak investigation: news had surfaced that OpenAI's new model used ‘looped transformer’technology, which the company wanted hidden. Investigators suspected the leak came via Signal messages between one researcher and outside contact Ryan Greenblatt, but both used disappearing messages—neither could prove innocence. Looped transformers let models perform hidden calculations before outputting chain-of-thought reasoning; the field has long warned this points toward unmonitorable models. All three researchers had previously publicly supported keeping chain-of-thought observable.

10:12 The evidence for firing the three was far weaker than stated
Disappearing messages are standard in tech and AI circles—you can't convict based on that alone, or everyone from CEO down would be suspect. The Information, which broke this story, has sourced OpenAI's internal secrets for years from investors, ex-employees, even casual conversation—not necessarily these three. Hundreds, possibly two hundred OpenAI employees could oppose looped transformers—this year alone, nearly 400 signed a petition demanding AI research slow for safety's sake. The host personally judges a Greenblatt leak highly unlikely; it doesn't fit his operating style at all. Conclusion: firing was probably error. The cost: the company will struggle to get candid employee input going forward, and the actual leaker may never be found.

12:52 Google DeepMind's contracts silence employees for life, not just at departure
According to BBC reporting, Google DeepMind's UK employment contracts forbid employees from publicly criticizing anything Google does—for life. The clause surfaced when a former employee tried to criticize Google's sale of AI to the US Defense Department (usable as long as DoD deems it legal), a deal that already prompted resignations over principle. This echoes the ‘non-disparagement agreement’scandal uncovered two years ago at OpenAI: former employees criticizing the company lost stock worth potentially tens of millions, and the clause itself demanded secrecy. After exposure, both OpenAI and Anthropic admitted to similar clauses and promised to drop them. Google DeepMind's version has no secrecy requirement and doesn't forfeit stock, but the lawsuit threat alone creates massive chilling effect on ordinary employees.

17:31 Speaking up inside requires public channels; speaking out requires going public
The host offers a graduated approach: to stay, calmly and rationally explain specific reasons for opposing a decision in public Slack channels colleagues will see, focusing on the few most critical points, not opposing everything reflexively, and staying open to being persuaded. If reasonable dissent gets no satisfactory response, escalate to publicly stating this makes you question the company's judgment and strategy—and that you're considering leaving. Still no results: submit a thorough resignation statement, then make your case public after departure. His reasoning: companies automate employee work faster by the year, so employees' bargaining power erodes over time. ‘If not now, when?’

21:39 Outside pressure reshapes corporate governance when insiders organize the pressure
Against OpenAI's plan to hollow out its nonprofit parent and charitable mission, the ‘Not For Private Gain’campaign had few participants but, paired with state attorneys general attention and broader coalition pressure, forced OpenAI to substantially revise: the OpenAI Foundation gained approximately 75 billion dollars in additional equity, and its Safety & Alignment Committee locked down decision rights over a range of safety questions. Similar: a 2024 campaign by former employees for ‘right to raise concerns’that became whistleblower protections in California's SB 53; continued reporting showing OpenAI publicly backing regulation while lobbying against it also pushed OpenAI to support SB 53-type rules and led President Greg Brockman to stop giving to the lobbying PAC ‘Leading the Future’.

item.title: Founders have only two peak focus windows daily; interruptions cost exponentially
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-a16z-创始人每天只有两段黄金专注期-被打断代价是指数级的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-a16z-创始人每天只有两段黄金专注期-被打断代价是指数级的/
item.description: Huberman says most people have only two or three truly productive focus windows per day; when that time is interrupted by unrelated matters, the loss isn't just those hours—it compounds exponentially against total output.
item.content:encoded:
Huberman says most people have only two or three truly productive focus windows per day; when that time is interrupted by unrelated matters, the loss isn't just those hours—it compounds exponentially against total output.

You get his complete daily schedule from wake to sleep, specific training protocols, and precise supplement dosing—dense information for anyone seeking a ready-made template. The casual conversation and self-deprecation can be skipped.

7:15 On workout days, take caffeine immediately after light exposure, not a half-hour later
When scheduling a workout, Huberman drinks caffeine-containing yerba mate immediately after sun exposure—not waiting even a minute, rather than following a fixed timetable. This means he ties caffeine intake to whether he's exercising that day, not his wake time. On rest days, he postpones caffeine later.

8:15 Staying injury-free for 35 years meant never chasing others' training routines
Huberman credits his health at 50 not to mastering specific training methods but to a 35-year discipline: never switching to another person's routine on impulse just because they challenged him to try it—the easiest path to injury. He does only movements his body feels good doing, like rowing machine and Airdyne sprints instead of cycling.

11:18 Two hard sets yield results with one-third the volume of conventional training
His strength structure is fixed: one light warm-up set, one medium set, then only two sets pushed to the edge of form breakdown, resting three to four minutes between. Per bodypart, just two or three movements. A multi-year soccer athlete testing his method reported it was one-third her previous volume but yielded results she found almost unbelievable.

21:35 Blue light sensitivity varies enormously; your skepticism might actually be justified
On pre-sleep blue light, Huberman notes enormous individual variation: some people spike cortisol and lose sleep from barely-visible light even through closed eyelids; others are completely insensitive, for reasons still unclear and independent of eye color. He mentions Marc Andreessen publicly saying he quit alcohol but dismisses blue-light protection entirely—Huberman acknowledges individual variation is real.

26:43 One supplement cuts infection risk by more than half in flu exposure studies
He cites a study exposing people to flu virus: those taking placebo infected at over 70%, while those taking N-acetylcysteine (NAC, a glutathione precursor) infected at just over 20%. He takes one dose daily himself, escalating to three when he feels illness coming or sees others sick.

30:55 Your social media phone needs to be locked away, not just silenced
Huberman admits social media is his weakest point: he keeps X and Instagram on a separate phone locked in a ‘super-prison-grade’ safe, accessible only at set times. He says this embarrasses him—ideally humans should self-regulate. He cites research: even with phone in a backpack, powered off, or under a chair, the brain burns extra cognitive resources to maintain equivalent focus. Phone completely absent, those resources release.

37:18 Peak cognitive windows contain exponentially more value than makeup work done later
For him, the two best cognitive windows are roughly 9:30 am to 12:30 pm and 4:35 pm to 7 pm—but the window varies per person, and he advises everyone to find theirs. The core warning: if work during that peak window is diverted to company-unrelated matters, the loss isn't just those three or four hours. Output during that window is exponentially higher than output from makeup work done later, and it also compresses personal time.

46:30 Startups are endurance races that demand weekly reset to avoid burnout
Huberman relays neuroscientist Bob Knight's early advice: first determine your daily maximum sustainable work output, then find a restorative method to reset once a week—Knight fishes, Huberman hikes and socializes. He notes that people who run on high stimulation continuously tend to be the ones who disappear last; sustaining intensity matters as much as the intensity itself.

item.title: War museums display heroes' photographs, but not a single victim's face
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-throughline-战争博物馆里挂满英雄照-却没有一张受害者/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-throughline-战争博物馆里挂满英雄照-却没有一张受害者/
item.description: Noah Adams observed in Belgrade's military museum: two hours of exhibits from ninth-century bows to World War II tanks, all heroic images, not one photograph of victims—making war itself seem like the normal state of affairs.
item.content:encoded:
Noah Adams observed in Belgrade's military museum: two hours of exhibits from ninth-century bows to World War II tanks, all heroic images, not one photograph of victims—making war itself seem like the normal state of affairs.

This is a tribute to NPR veteran broadcaster Noah Adams, reprising three of his pieces from 1993, 1998, and 2001. The density is light but the observation is sharp—a perfect listen for careful readers who appreciate close, writerly attention to detail.

1:04 War museums display heroes' photographs but never display victims' faces
When Noah Adams visited Yugoslavia's military museum at Karamagdan Park in Belgrade, fresh from a two-week reporting trip to Serbia, he found himself looking at two hours of exhibits spanning from ninth-century bows to World War II artillery and tanks. What struck him was the absence: only heroic images hung in the gallery; not a single photograph of a victim appeared. Combined with the daily news from the Bosnian War—young people dying, politicians speaking, relief organizations intervening, the cycle repeating—the museum seemed to suggest that war itself was simply the normal state of things.

4:13 Old men playing chess in the park harbor decades of unspeakable silence
In that same park, Adams watched elderly men playing chess with each other, neat in appearance and gentle with one another. He guessed that among them were men who, fifty years ago, had fought in what was called the ‘人民解放战争’ during World War II. But he acknowledged his own limitation: two weeks in Serbia was not enough to truly understand the Bosnian War. Instead, he turned to an American parallel. If a Serbian came to America, how would you explain that Gettysburg saw 40,000 deaths and Antietam 24,000? And he noticed something else: Serbs who publicly opposed the Bosnian War would, the moment Kosovo's Albanians came up in conversation, show a different look in their eyes altogether.

10:30 At age ten, a frightened horse dragged his father to his death
In 1998, during Nebraska's severe drought, Adams interviewed Glenn Osborn, a farmer born in 1919. Osborn recalled the dust storms of the Depression era: chickens would return to their coops in mid-afternoon because the air was full of ash; the sky turned dark as night. But there was heavier loss in his past. His mother died when he was five. At ten, he went with his father to a neighbor's to husk corn. A truck fitted with a canvas cover passed by, and the wind caught the canvas, startling the horses pulling it. His father ran after the horses, while young Glenn ran behind a box. The horses dragged his father to death. Sixty years later, when Osborn recounted this, he said it felt ‘就像昨天早上才发生的’as though it had happened only yesterday morning.

14:34 Farm crisis hotlines reopen when drought threatens farmers' mental survival
Drought destroys more than crops. It tears at farmers' mental states. Jim Osborn and his wife Lynn recalled that the farm crisis hotline—set up during the bank failures of the 1980s—was running again. Because many farmers were experiencing acute stress and crisis. Adams pressed: did the USDA really operate a phone crisis line because farmers were considering suicide? The answer was yes. Lynn added that when such moments came, it was usually the farmer's wife who made the call; the farmers themselves preferred not to talk face-to-face with anyone. They would rather go home and sit alone facing a wall in silent anguish.

17:40 No customers at the hardware store means the drought is here
Benkelman, population 1,193, depends entirely on the agriculture surrounding it. Erma Johnson, who runs the hardware store, explained that she carries roughly one hundred accounts on credit, and nearly all of them are farmers. You don't need to check the weather forecast; just see if customers walk in the door. If they don't, there's a drought. Pat Rotherman, the town bank's president, gave harder numbers: this year, he estimated that ten to fifteen percent of small farmers wouldn't make it—they would have to sell their land and exit farming. In normal years, that figure should be zero. The bank's approach was to try to keep them, not push them into bankruptcy.

19:44 Free barbecue night, and then the rain came that changed everything
On the third night of the county fair, the wind picked up. The American Legion flag they'd just bought whipped tight. Clouds piled high to the north, west, and south. It was Free Barbecue Night: a thousand people stood in line for grilled beef, onions, and potatoes. When thunder rolled, nobody left early—nobody wanted to go, even as the fair had to close ahead of schedule and the concert moved into the high school auditorium. The next morning at breakfast, farmers swapped rain stories. One household had measured one-quarter inch; another two inches. Almost every farm had two rain gauges to cross-check. This single rainfall became the week's only big news in Benkelman—not fit to print in the Denver Post, but the only story that truly mattered to the town.

22:50 The researchers themselves won't say their gene edits are safe for cats
In 2001, Adams interviewed David Avner, president of Transgenic Pets, a company developing cats through genetic engineering that wouldn't trigger human allergies. The plan was to disable the gene that makes the protein in cats' sebaceous glands that causes the allergy. Adams asked the obvious question: over the course of evolution, might cats actually need this gene? Avner called it redundant protein, said they'd researched it for ten to fifteen years, and believed it should be fine. But Adams caught a crucial detail: when the same question was put to Jerry Yang, a genetics professor at the University of Connecticut who'd worked on the project, Yang's answer was: ‘我们希望不会’We hope it won't. Adams noted directly that this sounded nothing like confidence.

23:50 Hypoallergenic cats would be priced from $750 to $1,000 each
For this technology still in development, Avner provided specific commercial projections and pricing: the company hoped to breed the first hypoallergenic cats by 2003 and, in the early years of mass production, bring the price down to $750 to $1,000 per cat—affordable for ordinary households. He positioned the technology as a paradigm shift in allergy treatment: instead of managing immune responses with antihistamines and weekly desensitization shots, you could simply remove the allergen source itself.

item.title: Polls aren't undercounting Republicans—they're overcorrecting from past misses
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-oddlots-民调不是在低估共和党-而是在怕错而过度修正/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-oddlots-民调不是在低估共和党-而是在怕错而过度修正/
item.description: A Maine poll used a ‘likely voter model’ to compress Democrats' raw 9-point lead to 2; Nate Silver says it's self-protection after 2016, not math.
item.content:encoded:
A Maine poll used a ‘likely voter model’ to compress Democrats' raw 9-point lead to 2; Nate Silver says it's self-protection after 2016, not math.

To understand how weak Trump's support truly is, whether polls deserve trust, and if AI can replace real-world polling, this episode packs information throughout.

2:04 Trump's approval hits lows unseen since Truman's era
Trump's approval sits around 37%—Nate Silver notes this is the worst approval rating for a sitting president at a midterm since Truman in 1946. Compare 2018: Trump's approval was higher then and gas was cheaper, yet Republicans still lost 41 House seats. He describes this election as ‘caught between a rock and a hard place’—the environment strongly favors Democrats, but to win the Senate, Democrats must flip Texas, Kansas, Alaska, and South Carolina: deep-red states where victory is mathematically necessary but a long shot.

4:09 Trump has exited campaign ads but seized the spotlight anyway
The clearest sign this is a referendum on Trump: Republican campaign ads have stopped mentioning him, Republican podcasts no longer discuss him. Yet Trump himself wants to grab center stage—he endorsed Texas's Ken Paxton and insisted on escalating toward conflict with Iran, moves that flipped a Senate map that could have been close into Democratic territory.

6:10 Polls underestimated Democrats when Trump wasn't on the ballot
Polls have systematically underestimated Trump himself in recent elections (2016, 2020, 2024), but in races where Trump isn't on the ballot—like last year's New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial races—polls badly underestimated Democrats. One explanation: Trump mobilizes hard-to-reach, infrequent voters who won't turn out for downstream candidates like Kansas's Roger Marshall or Texas's Ken Paxton.

15:19 A Maine poll artificially compressed a 9-point lead into 2
Maine's Marist poll showed Democrat Troy Jackson ahead by 9 points in raw results, then dropped to just 2 points after applying the ‘likely voter model’; the gubernatorial lead fell from 11 points to zero. Nate Silver: the math doesn't add up—it's not that the model computed this result, but that pollsters chose a palatable number and reverse-engineered the parameters to reach it.

18:22 AI cannot serve as a real-world polling substitute through synthetic respondents
On the idea of using AI to generate synthetic respondents for polls, Nate Silver is blunt: polling is one of the few remaining sources of real-world data, and can't be outsourced to AI. He gives an example—ask a model to generate a ‘synthetic Latino respondent’ and 99% of synthetic answers will say they love soccer. It's like asking Claude to pick a number from 0 to 10 and it always picks 7: models output stereotype averages, not the messy reality where voters disagree even with themselves.

21:24 Gerrymandering to win more seats can backfire and cost seats
Nate Silver introduces the political term ‘dummymander’—a gerrymander designed to flip more seats that winds up costing your party seats instead. Florida's DeSantis drew maps based on presidential-year benchmarks and didn't account for this cycle's D+9 national environment; Texas Republicans bet Latino voters in South Texas had shifted red—if that gamble fails, the maps could backfire.

27:31 Campaign spending on ads faces steeply diminishing returns
On whether campaigns should spend money on ads or ground game, Nate Silver says ad returns diminish sharply. He cites Sam Bankman-Fried, who poured $10 million into an Oregon House primary without the candidate's consent, only to have voters bombarded with mail and spooked by backing from an ‘eccentric crypto billionaire’—the candidate lost badly.

37:46 AI compressed two and a half days of work into fifteen minutes
Last year, coding the complex NFL playoff tiebreaker rules by hand took Nate Silver two and a half days and still had bugs and missing rules. Now GPT or Claude handles it in fifteen minutes with code ten times faster. But he warns AI introduces subtle bugs—their football model once had a scoring loop that pointed backward in time, so 2026 ratings affected 1900 ratings, bizarre.

item.title: A four-year-old's months-long repeated expressions of sadness merit serious attention
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-secureattach-四岁孩子反复说自己难过长达数月-值得认真对待/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-secureattach-四岁孩子反复说自己难过长达数月-值得认真对待/
item.description: A four-year-old boy has spent months repeatedly saying he is sad without being able to explain why; a psychologist says this warrants professional evaluation—depression in young children is rare but real, and treatable.
item.content:encoded:
A four-year-old boy has spent months repeatedly saying he is sad without being able to explain why; a psychologist says this warrants professional evaluation—depression in young children is rare but real, and treatable.

For parents uncertain whether their child's emotional expression is normal, it offers concrete criteria for deciding whether to seek professional help—not generic reassurance.

4:06 Months of sadness is the key signal
This mother's four-year-old son has spent months repeatedly saying he is sad, sometimes the moment he wakes up. Rebecca Hershberg notes that even four-year-olds—and younger children—can experience depression. While young children rarely meet the formal diagnostic criteria for depression, a duration of ‘months’ is already a long span for a four-year-old. Add the mother's own long struggle with anxiety and depression: that family-level genetic loading is a variable beyond parenting style's control. With both factors present, Hershberg recommends direct professional evaluation rather than waiting for the podcast to air before offering guidance.

7:15 Depression in young children is rare but treatable
Host Sarah Bren cautions against panic at the word ‘depression’—it is genuinely rare in young children, and even if evaluation confirms it, it is entirely treatable. She frames the process as elimination, not crisis, aiming for parents to neither dismiss the signal nor fear seeking help. Her view: failing to screen is the riskier choice.

8:18 Appetite, sleep, and peer relationships tell the story
There is no single formula for whether to intervene, but Rebecca gives concrete dimensions to observe: the child's appetite, sleep, and how they interact with peers. She even recommends ruling out seemingly unrelated physical factors—children with prolonged low mood sometimes need thyroid screening. The pediatrician is the easiest first stop, though most are not mental-health experts and can only make preliminary judgments before deciding on referral.

9:20 The change from baseline matters more than the emotion itself
Sarah adds that what matters is not whether a child says ‘sad’ but whether this represents a departure from their baseline—a shift in how they engage with the world, versus a temperamental constant. Typical departure signals are changes in relationships, loss of interest, and giving up things they once loved. The mother's description partly fits this pattern.

11:28 Age thresholds matter when finding a child therapist
Rebecca cautions that many who claim to do child therapy only accept ages six and up. Therapists who actually treat preschoolers should explicitly state expertise with young and toddler-age children. For this age group, therapy is nearly always play-based—stories, stuffed animals, puppets, not sitting down to talk. Parents must actively confirm the therapist's experience covers this age.

16:42 Play therapy works for internalizing problems, not externalizing ones
Rebecca distinguishes two types: children who internalize emotions—sadness, anxiety, trauma—the ‘internalizing’ problems play therapy excels at; and those with ‘externalizing’ behavior problems like aggression or impulsivity, where play therapy struggles to transfer learning from the room to the world, often requiring family-system intervention. She urges parents to be ‘informed consumers’ because some therapists claim to handle all types.

19:50 Parental presence is the safety net that makes therapy work
For children this young, Rebecca more often uses joint parent-child play therapy rather than having the child meet alone. She calls parental presence a ‘warm handoff’: the child experiences the therapist as safe, with the parent as a reference point. When discussing painful material, knowing both mother and therapist are ‘there’ lets the young child enter genuine emotional work with a stranger.

item.title: Glanders still has no vaccine; culling all infected animals remains the only control method
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-tpwky-鼻疽至今没有疫苗-防控唯一办法就是扑杀所有感染动物/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-tpwky-鼻疽至今没有疫苗-防控唯一办法就是扑杀所有感染动物/
item.description: This bacterium, which obligately parasitizes equines, kills over 90% of those infected, is inherently antibiotic-resistant, and after more than a century of human research, the only effective approach remains: discover and cull.
item.content:encoded:
This bacterium, which obligately parasitizes equines, kills over 90% of those infected, is inherently antibiotic-resistant, and after more than a century of human research, the only effective approach remains: discover and cull.

Obscure pathogen education with high information density but inclined toward curiosity value; well-researched historical detail on Civil War cavalry plague; better suited for curiosity-driven listening than policy reference.

3:05 A doctor took three weeks to admit he had contracted glanders
In 1911, a Punjab Veterinary College researcher was already familiar with the appearance of typical glanders cultures—he used this evidence every year to order the culling of infected horses. But when the same bacterial colony appeared in a culture from his own wound, he convinced himself ‘it must be a mistake,’ and even destroyed the already-prepared sample, until the disease progressed to undeniable severity. He subsequently underwent 45 operations (27 under general anesthesia), with illness lasting from March 1911 until June 1913 before recovery—and he relapsed once after that.

9:40 The lethal glanders bacterium carries roughly 1200 fewer genes than its relative
Burkholderia mallei, the pathogen of glanders, is an obligate parasite that can barely survive independently outside its host—a stark contrast to the related Burkholderia pseudomallei (which causes melioidosis and freely survives and reproduces in soil), whose genome is roughly 1200 genes larger than mallei. Though mallei has ‘degenerated’ into an obligate parasite, that same adaptation makes it vulnerable to deliberate eradication across entire regions, as happened in the twentieth century.

20:57 Glanders is never treated; infected animals are only culled
When animals contract glanders, the World Organisation for Animal Health recommends direct culling rather than antibiotic treatment—the bacterium is inherently resistant to most antibiotics. More extreme: any individual exposed to an infected animal faces continuous monitoring, and at the first symptom has the same fate as the animal. The approach is crude, but it is the only method that actually works; the cost is that no one can now say what the true natural mortality rate is in infected animals, because almost every case ends by human termination before it could run its natural course.

24:00 Treated humans still die in forty percent to fifty percent of cases
After human infection with glanders, the untreated mortality rate exceeds 90%; the pneumonic form typically proves fatal within 10 to 30 days. Even with treatment, mortality remains as high as 40%-50%. Because the disease is so rare, the Infectious Diseases Society of America has no official treatment guideline; existing protocols amount to expert consensus only: at least 10 to 14 days of intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, followed by six months to a year of oral antibiotics, without necessarily requiring drainage of internal abscesses—entirely unlike standard care for most bacterial infections.

34:21 A student died dissecting a glanders-infected horse, yet the professor blamed cadaverous poison
Into the nineteenth century, whether glanders was contagious remained a centuries-old dispute in veterinary medicine. In 1817, a veterinary student accidentally cut his hand while dissecting a glanders-infected horse and died shortly after. The professor investigating took samples from the student's body and inoculated them into two donkeys, both of which became infected with glanders—yet he concluded that glanders was not contagious and the student had died of ‘cadaverous poisoning’ (which was actually glanders itself). This dispute only ended in the mid-nineteenth century through a series of experimental infections.

41:35 A single Union cavalry depot lost seventeen thousand horses to glanders in one year
During the Civil War, the Union lost over 284,000 horses and mules in just the first two years. To centralize supply, both sides built massive depots holding tens of thousands of horses—the Giesboro depot in Washington, D.C. could hold 30,000 horses at peak capacity. Horses greet each other nose-to-nose and share feeding troughs, providing ideal conditions for glanders transmission. From January 1864 to April 1865, that single depot lost 17,000 horses to disease alone—on one day, over 180 died. The Confederacy fared worse: one depot received 7,000 horses and sent only 1,000 to the battlefield.

48:43 A Tier 1 bioterror agent, glanders infected a microbiologist in a lab this century
During World War II, Japanese forces deployed glanders in biological attacks against horses, civilians, and prisoners of war; there are also reports that the Soviet Union deliberately infected mujahideen horses during the Afghan War in the early 1980s. In 2000, the United States formally classified glanders as a Tier 1 select agent, placing it alongside smallpox, plague, anthrax, and Ebola. Ironically, that same year, a 33-year-old microbiologist at the U.S. Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases accidentally contracted glanders while researching it—he frequently worked without gloves, marking the first recorded human case in English medical literature since 1949; he survived after six months of treatment.

51:51 Vaccine research remains at animal testing; glanders persists in multiple regions
Glanders has been eradicated from vast regions including the EU, Australia, and the United States, but through culling and isolation alone, not vaccination—animal vaccine research remains at early experimental stages, without even Phase 1 human trials. Meanwhile, glanders continues to cause sporadic cases and outbreaks in South Asia, Southwest Asia, and North Africa: a 2010 Tehran Zoo outbreak killed 4 lions and 1 tiger; Nepal's first confirmed case came in 2022; Brazil reported 120 cases across 43 municipalities between 2020 and 2024.

item.title: Parents' accommodation of avoidance makes anxiety harder to treat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-asklisa-父母越是心疼着接送孩子逃避-焦虑就越难治好/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-asklisa-父母越是心疼着接送孩子逃避-焦虑就越难治好/
item.category: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens
item.description: The relief from avoidance teaches the brain ‘I can't handle this,’ making escape likelier next time. The evidence-based approach is gradual exposure to discomfort—a framework that works equally for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder.
item.content:encoded:
The relief from avoidance teaches the brain ‘I can't handle this,’ making escape likelier next time. The evidence-based approach is gradual exposure to discomfort—a framework that works equally for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder.

Through a real letter, it distinguishes three diagnostic markers of clinical anxiety from everyday nervousness, and reveals well-intentioned parental responses that inadvertently perpetuate the anxiety cycle.

3:08 Three markers distinguish everyday nervousness from diagnosable anxiety
Clinicians apply three hard metrics: functional impairment (whether anxiety disrupts daily life, like the letter-writer's daughter being picked up from school repeatedly mid-day), degree of suffering (crying, anguish), and duration (persisting weeks rather than resolving in days). All three together signal need for professional intervention—not mere introversion or temporary setback.

5:08 We use one word for two separate psychological conditions
Psychology should have distinct vocabularies for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder, but it doesn't. The word ‘anxiety’ both flattens everything and pathologizes it all. Elkins uses a water-glass metaphor: everyone is born with some baseline anxiety water; it serves a function, keeping you safe (look both ways before crossing, brush teeth before a date). Only when the glass overflows—due to genetics and other factors—does clinical anxiety disorder emerge.

13:23 The temporary relief of avoidance teaches permanent anxiety
Each time discomfort is escaped rather than faced, the brain learns: feeling better came from running away, therefore ‘I cannot handle this.’ Next time something similar arises, anxiety intensifies and avoidance becomes likelier. In the letter, the girl ducking into the bathroom and being picked up looks like relief to parents—but it reinforces ‘I'm alone, unloved, friendless.’

14:23 Exposure therapy starts with the smallest manageable discomfort
The gold-standard psychological treatment for anxiety is exposure therapy—ranking situations by distress level from least to most, starting with the easiest (greeting one classmate in the classroom), then gradually climbing, not throwing the child into full-day school as the first step. Elkins jokes her program ‘isn't a spa’—kids typically feel worse at first, which is precisely how you know the method is working.

22:45 Years of avoidance can transform ordinary anxiety into phobia
Elkins shared her own story: years in Boston and Manhattan meant she never needed to drive—not deliberate avoidance, but functionally she stopped. When she finally had to, while pregnant and terrified, it happened in Massachusetts, notorious for dangerous roads. Her solution: drive repeatedly until it felt boring—a finish line everyone can reach, but only after tolerating initial discomfort.

28:06 Parents are the real leverage point in treating child anxiety
Therapeutic rapport accounts for up to 50% of clinical outcomes, but even if a child refuses to see a therapist, parents aren't helpless. The most exciting progress of the past decade is ‘parent-directed’ treatment like Yale's SPACE program: the patient is the child, but the therapist primarily coaches parents, helping them spot well-meaning responses that accidentally reinforce the child's anxiety cycle.

32:21 Accommodation motivated by kindness perpetuates the anxiety cycle
Accommodation means parents adjusting their own behavior to reduce the child's distress—no parent sets out to fan the flames, but anxiety hijacks parents' deepest instinct to ease pain, making accommodation invisible and continuous. Research shows the more parents accommodate, the worse children's anxiety disorder tends to become; and those same parents suffer more depression, anxiety, and stress themselves—bad news for everyone.

38:35 Switching schools won't help without addressing the avoidance pattern
When parents wrestle with whether to transfer their child, Elkins is cautious, because anxiety is an ‘opportunist’—it will seize any chance to destroy one lifestyle and escape to the next. Without first addressing the underlying anxiety cycle and family accommodation patterns, a new school just teaches avoidance as the go-to coping strategy. Transfer should only come first if there's genuine, ongoing bullying, harassment, discrimination, or safety threats.

item.title: Two-year-old defiance isn't a broken bond—it's emotion doing repair work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-unruffled-两岁娃的疯狂抵抗不是亲子关系出问题-而是情绪在自愈/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-unruffled-两岁娃的疯狂抵抗不是亲子关系出问题-而是情绪在自愈/
item.description: When toddlers say no to everything—getting in the car, bathing, holding hands at crossings—it's because they've weathered massive changes with no sense of control; the answer isn't more choices but tighter, earlier boundaries.
item.content:encoded:
When toddlers say no to everything—getting in the car, bathing, holding hands at crossings—it's because they've weathered massive changes with no sense of control; the answer isn't more choices but tighter, earlier boundaries.

Two real letters show end-to-end resistance at boarding the car, bathing, holding hands, and bedtime, with ready-to-use response tactics.

5:10 Emotional storms are not signals of relationship breakdown
Her daughter experienced housing moves, then a new daycare within three weeks. Janet notes that same-aged and older children create more uncertainty than adults do—adding another source of stress. This is a ‘transition crisis,’ not a relationship problem. Better housing or warmer caregiving wouldn't prevent it. The trigger is loss of familiarity, regardless of circumstances.

6:11 Children who hold it together most need permission to collapse
Janet distinguishes two response patterns: fragile children break down directly, while determined, sensitive children ‘hold, hold, hold’—using continuous resistance to fight the out-of-control feeling. When parents worry about resistance and treat it as a red flag, they undermine the firmness these children need to release fear and sadness. Firmness is the container that enables the release.

9:22 During transitions, tighten boundaries rather than expand choices
The parent has been minimizing restrictions and offering choices, but Janet names a counterintuitive rule: in high-stakes transitions—boarding the car, crossing streets—children actually need fewer choices and earlier, clearer boundaries, not more autonomy. Set boundaries earlier and the resistance drops, because she won't have to wrestle alone with that feeling of lost control.

11:25 Set a window, then step in directly; no open delays
Specific tactics: at boarding time, offer a few seconds to choose, then directly buckle her in without prolonging the request loop. If she stands in the stroller, lift her without repeated verbal requests. When she heads the wrong way or toward danger, hold her hand or pick her up. Early intervention, more protection. At this stage, it won't hurt her—it's exactly what she needs.

14:28 Let kids choose bathing, but allow bedtime meltdowns
Bathing is a voluntary activity. If she refuses, wiping off works fine—let her choose. But stop dangerous or excessive behavior immediately by lifting her out. Bedtime is different. Children often save a full day's accumulated frustrations for this moment. Parents shouldn't add more books or extend delays to soothe. Instead, clearly allow the breakdown—this is exactly when she most needs to release.

15:31 Managing conflict with firmness and empathy strengthens the bond
The parent worried ‘the relationship will revolve around these conflicts.’ Janet's answer: when you meet intense feeling with both firmness and empathy, conflict actually fortifies rather than erodes the bond. It's not a warm, close moment. It's something deeper: the child confirming ‘I can have a huge feeling, and you're still here keeping me safe.’ It's one of the most connective things that happens between you.

17:34 Dramatic tears at separation signal secure attachment, not anxiety
Mom started a new job; dad now does daycare drop-off. Her goodbye to mom is intensely theatrical. Janet reframes this: when a child releases strong emotion at parting, it means there's enough safety with that parent to express pain. Dad may not see this intensity because the child experiences separations differently with him. This dramatic release is worth reading as a vote of confidence, not as evidence separation went wrong.

22:50 Asking for water and the bathroom is stalling the crash
The second letter: son goes from calm to suddenly ‘flipping a switch’ at bedtime, then repeatedly requesting water, the bathroom, finally collapsing in tears wanting to leave the room. Parent isn't sure whether reading more books soothes or teaches ‘emotions are scary; we can't handle them.’ Janet's suggestion: weave those routine requests into the presleep sequence, then you can confidently refuse extras. Then receive the tears as healthy release. The calmer parents are with this as normal, the faster it passes.

item.title: The biggest engineering challenge in legal AI is not models—it's data you can never see
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-latentspace-法律ai最大的工程难题不是模型-是永远看不到真实数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-latentspace-法律ai最大的工程难题不是模型-是永远看不到真实数据/
item.description: Most client data isn't even visible to the law firm itself. Legora's evals team has to guess what lawyers actually do, working only with classified and rewritten synthetic data.
item.content:encoded:
Most client data isn't even visible to the law firm itself. Legora's evals team has to guess what lawyers actually do, working only with classified and rewritten synthetic data.

High information density. Shows exactly how enterprise AI companies do evals, model selection, and frontline support in zero-visibility environments, with minimal filler.

10:43 The hardest hire: lawyers from top firms who can code
Legora's evals team blends engineers and lawyers, plus a distinct group of legal engineers—lawyers with CS backgrounds who spent three to four years at top firms. They're the hardest intersection to fill. Jacob calls them the company's hardest hire, but they're invaluable: they run evals and directly shape product design because they use the product every day and see clients every day. They become force multipliers who can summon a hundred-person expert pool to reshape the product.

14:30 AI may not be able to fix the law firm partnership model
Partnership exists because law firms' only capital is human capital—lose people, lose the firm, so just make people shareholders. Jacob argues AI should let firms codify experience and methods into reusable systems—say, a self-iterating knowledge graph—building firm-owned assets independent of any person. Instead, partners are paid by eating what they hunt, so encoding experience costs them clients. And those assets don't follow you when you leave partnership. The incentive misalignment has no answer yet.

16:45 Junior lawyers aren't disappearing—they're splitting into two tiers
The host suggests paralegals are obsolete, junior lawyers are obsolete. Jacob pushes back: that's not what they're seeing. He uses engineers as analogy: a great engineer is worth far more than two years ago because AI multiplies output; same for lawyers. Good junior lawyers become more valuable because AI lets them produce more, higher-quality work. This split always existed—now it's amplified, not the whole group gone.

26:40 Build evals when you cannot see a single user's real data
Legora's biggest engineering problem isn't model ability—it's that you can't see what customers do with the product. Data stays under lock. Often it doesn't even belong to the law firm; it belongs to their clients. Looking is forbidden. The company's only move is its evals team: guess, approximate real scenarios, build those guesses into test sets. Rewritten, anonymized synthetic traces are the only workaround. The stricter the anonymization, the weaker the signal. Jacob calls this the most maddening knot in the business.

28:50 Three years ago law firms wouldn't touch AWS
Legora runs entirely on Azure. Early in the company, law firm customers flatly didn't trust AWS or Google—no one had audited them. But Microsoft was already Office 365's vendor, so it had passed their audit test. Azure became the only option. In three years, that cloud skepticism nearly evaporated. Talk of private deployment vanished too. Legal's cloud migration was compressed into three years by AI pressure.

43:00 Legal engineers don't write code; frontline engineers do
Legora splits on-site support in two: legal engineers are big-firm alumni who know the product and customer workflows—they configure like power users, no code. Forward deployed engineers actually write code and hit customer APIs, usually serial entrepreneurs or large-company veterans. Big customers' custom needs go to legal engineers first; if they can't handle it and it needs product change or deep integration, escalate to forward engineers. This two-tier split lets the company staff big customers without assigning a full engineering team per customer.

50:00 Twenty engineers to beat everyone—he gave up that idea
Jacob once planned to keep the company to twenty engineers forever and beat much larger competitors. The team is now a hundred; he still thinks it's short. Hard competition and customer demand killed the minimalism. Now his thinking is different: collapse the product to a few core primitives—Lists, Projects, Agent. Customers think the company builds many things. Actually they're combinations of those three. He's even imagining a future where agents are themselves APIs, one agent call instead of a full interface to maintain.

1:03:50 Will large model companies squeeze out companies like Legora?
Anthropic and OpenAI have already squeezed out startups dependent on their models—once in code, once in search. Will legal be next? Jacob's read: no. Model companies must cover all enterprise knowledge work at once—law, data analysis, sales, finance. They can't go deep enough in one vertical. Small customers can use Claude for light legal work. But a $400 million acquisition? Enterprises pick the specialist.

item.title: Robot startups that won by selling hourly rates, not AI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-a16z-机器人创业公司不卖ai-只卖-时薪16美元-这句话/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-a16z-机器人创业公司不卖ai-只卖-时薪16美元-这句话/
item.description: When Tutor pitches to first-time robot buyers, it never mentions models or AI—just one number: $16 an hour. The strategy reflects a vast market gap: America deploys only 38,000 industrial robots annually, leaving 90% of factories untouched.
item.content:encoded:
When Tutor pitches to first-time robot buyers, it never mentions models or AI—just one number: $16 an hour. The strategy reflects a vast market gap: America deploys only 38,000 industrial robots annually, leaving 90% of factories untouched.

From a company that has actually shipped robots to hundreds of factories. Unlike most robotics startups, it focuses on hardware, sales cycles, and supply chains—not model innovation.

3:13 Start with robot deployment, not model training
Josh observes that 99% of robotics startups begin with a model or data insight, but few ask what a robot actually needs to do. Tutor inverts this. Even if perfect software could connect 8 billion humans' physical intelligence to any machine, robots still wouldn't exist, supply chains wouldn't exist, and customers wouldn't exist—because robotics remains a cottage industry even in manufacturing and logistics. So Tutor deploys robots in the real world first, then builds datasets, models, and supply chains from that experience.

9:27 There's no internet for physical labor, so build one
Josh explains the company name by contrasting social media and email—natural human behaviors that inadvertently created a training dataset for LLMs—with physical work, which leaves no digital record. When Josh picks up his coffee cup, no one records the pressure or angle his fingers used. Tutor's solution isn't to invent physical reasoning from scratch. Instead, it deploys robots into the real world where human remote operators (the "tutors") teach machines new tasks. This amounts to building an internet for robot training data, and the process itself generates economic value by making customer goods cheaper.

16:47 America deployed 38,000 industrial robots last year. That's it.
Josh offers a sobering comparison: U.S. factories and warehouses took delivery of just 38,000 industrial robots in 2025—a volume so small that even one successful humanoid robot model would barely register statistically. The problem runs deeper than quantity. Robotics OEMs like Fanuc and ABB make machines either overseas or for systems integrators handling fast-repeat tasks—not designed around the choices needed to work with advanced LLMs. Tutor had no choice but to design and manufacture its own hardware rather than source off the shelf.

18:54 Two robots handle 80–90% of warehouse and factory jobs
Tutor makes only two models. Cassie is a single-arm robot with a suction gripper—a "workhorse" powered by a foundation model with 200M–400M parameters. It handles heavy pallets and cartons, solving the labor problem of turnover (workers average 55 years old and quit within three months). Sunny is a wheeled (not legged, because factory floors are polished) industrial humanoid robot engineered to run continuously for three to ten years at human speed and reliability, with industrial-grade collaborative safety. Josh claims these two robots cover 80 to 90 percent of manufacturing and logistics work.

23:58 The sales call opens with an hourly rate, not a model
Tutor's customers are almost entirely first-time robot buyers—people familiar with older automation who assume robots can't apply to their business. Breaking through means abandoning the pitch about AI, models, or tutors. Instead, Tutor calls and asks, "Have you considered a robot at $16 an hour?"—a proposition they've never heard. This alignment of incentives lets Tutor move multiples faster than traditional industrial automation. First call to signature: 40–60 days. Signature to robot running on site: roughly 40 days. Installation often happens in a day or even hours.

30:10 Betting on a big customer and custom work is how robot startups die
Josh has observed this pattern repeat five to ten times: a research-heavy robotics company lands an LOI from a large customer, spends two years building a hyper-customized system, and it either doesn't work or the customer's problem disappears. The company dies. His lesson: work with diverse small and medium customers. That constraint—far from being a weakness—forces the company to build a true general-purpose robotic body and platform, not a Rube Goldberg machine built for a single buyer.

32:16 Demand shifts entirely when factory-built homes undercut site-built by just 1 percent
Josh recalls an example from a Wisconsin housing factory worker: factory-built homes currently cost 5% more than site construction. But the instant factory construction becomes just 1% cheaper—even fractionally—developers will shift all demand to the factory model. He uses this to argue that robots don't unlock linearly declining costs. Cross a critical threshold and entire industries flip. The same logic applies to materials recovery at landfills and similar markets where cost inflection points trigger structural shifts in where work gets done.

39:20 China's bet on yesterday's automation may be a long-term miscalculation
When pressed on how robotics will reshape factory location and regional manufacturing patterns, Josh pivots to geopolitics. China invested heavily in the previous generation of industrial automation, and it paid off handsomely. But over the long term, it may be a massive mistake. The U.S. is now undertaking greenfield automation using general-purpose robots without tearing out old lines first—an advantage China lacks. Josh acknowledges that supply chains remain deeply linked: Chinese and American firms both invest in each other's markets and build their own capabilities. Tutor itself is moving more component supply vertically back to its Watertown factory because the company has become one of the largest demand sources for certain OEMs.

item.title: Two traders cornered the onion market and forced Congress to permanently ban onion futures
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-stuffmissed-两个农民囤光洋葱操纵期货-让国会专门立法禁掉了洋葱期货/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-stuffmissed-两个农民囤光洋葱操纵期货-让国会专门立法禁掉了洋葱期货/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The two conspired to buy nearly all Chicago onions, forced distributors to sign a secret deal, then shorted the market and crashed prices to historic lows, leading Congress to permanently ban onion futures trading.
item.content:encoded:
The two conspired to buy nearly all Chicago onions, forced distributors to sign a secret deal, then shorted the market and crashed prices to historic lows, leading Congress to permanently ban onion futures trading.

The story itself is absurd, but the real lesson is this: proving market manipulation intent is harder in court than proving the harm it caused.

4:04 Futures were supposed to stabilize prices, but the data didn't support it
The classic justification for futures trading is that it lets farmers and wholesalers lock in prices early, making markets more stable and prices less volatile. But the show cites a 1956 Commodity Exchange Authority report showing that from 1929 to 1956, onion prices actually swung wider than many other commodities with futures markets. The stabilizing effect futures were supposed to provide never materialized for onions.

13:24 The two conspired to corner nearly all Chicago onions
Vince Kasuga, a floor trader with onion-farming roots, and Sam Siegel, an exchange member, quietly bought 928 November onion futures contracts in late 1955, accounting for 45% of that month's open interest. When the contracts settled on November 30, Kasuga alone held 262 railcars of onions—over 7.8 million pounds—half of Chicago's entire onion supply. Including outstanding contracts, by early 1956 the two controlled roughly 1,000 railcars, nearly equal to Chicago's entire cash onion supply.

16:28 They pressured distributors into a secret deal
Kasuga and Siegel didn't stop at hoarding. They approached 13 onion distributors in Chicago and threatened to dump their entire stockpile on the market—crushing everyone's prices—unless the distributors bought onions from them at their set price. The distributors eventually agreed to purchase 287 railcars for $1.60 per bag, totaling $275,000, with the condition that Kasuga and Siegel would not make any additional deliveries for the rest of the season. Both sides understood the deal had to remain secret.

18:34 After the deal fell apart, they shorted the market
In January and February 1956, distributors began suspecting Kasuga and Siegel had reneged on their promise. All but one refused further payments or deliveries. The two then secretly shorted March onion futures, selling 858 railcars—44.3% of that month's open interest. They were the only ones holding short positions; everyone else was long. Distributor Dave Slinger later testified that Kasuga even called him urging him to short as well, saying the market would collapse to 50 cents in minutes if they all acted together.

21:37 Onion prices hit historic lows—the sack cost more than the onions
When the March 1956 futures settled, the market was flooded with onions. Prices plummeted to as low as 10 cents, closing at 15 cents—an all-time low for the exchange, beating the previous record of 43 cents. According to Kasuga's nephew in an NPR interview, a mesh sack for onions cost 20 cents to make, yet a full sack sold for only 10 cents. The show notes this crash wasn't purely artificial—Texas onions unexpectedly harvested early that same period, which also drove the collapse.

26:43 Intent is harder to prove than harm
The Commodity Exchange Authority's hearing found that Kasuga and Siegel's December 1955 coercion of distributors and March 1956 short-selling to suppress prices both constituted illegal market manipulation, even though they claimed they only wanted to stabilize prices. But regarding their massive November futures purchases, the ruling acknowledged that manipulation was common on the onion exchange and ultimately found insufficient evidence of manipulative intent—that charge was dropped. The line between legal trading and manipulation can be blurry.

27:44 Congress directly prohibited onion futures despite existing market manipulation laws
After the 1960 ruling, Kasuga, Siegel, and National Produce Distributors were barred from all futures markets for 10 months. But the bigger consequence came earlier: on August 28, 1958, a bill introduced by Representative Gerald Ford—pushed by affected Michigan onion farmers and signed by President Eisenhower—directly prohibited onion futures trading, even though market manipulation was already illegal under existing law. The Chicago Mercantile Exchange sued claiming it was unconstitutional; they lost and didn't appeal. The law remains in effect today.

31:49 Movie futures: the only other commodity banned after onions
After the onion case, commodity futures saw another scandal in 1963: the soybean oil swindle. Tony DeAngelis substituted water for soybean oil, stockpiled it as collateral, and manipulated soybean futures, ultimately serving 10 years. Regulatively, Congress passed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission Act in 1974, and the Dodd-Frank Act addressed the 2008 crisis in 2010. But trying to legislatively ban a specific futures contract has succeeded only once since onions: the 2010 movie futures ban, prompted by the Motion Picture Association's lobbying. In the same law, onions and movie box office remain the only two commodities explicitly prohibited from futures trading.

item.title: Scientists tricked a rat's brain into thinking salt water tasted good
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-mindscape-科学家让大鼠的大脑-骗-自己盐水很好喝/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-mindscape-科学家让大鼠的大脑-骗-自己盐水很好喝/
item.description: Researchers used optogenetics to amplify reward-signal neurons in rat brains so that when the rat drank salt water it hated, the brain still judged 'this was good'—sensory input and reward signals can be directly severed.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers used optogenetics to amplify reward-signal neurons in rat brains so that when the rat drank salt water it hated, the brain still judged 'this was good'—sensory input and reward signals can be directly severed.

The content spans behavioral game theory experiments, brain imaging research, and optogenetic manipulation, with high information density and little filler, though the second half leans into neuroscience details.

3:45 Rationality is economics' limiting case, not how humans actually decide
Camerer describes the utility-maximization model as a ‘limiting case’ in economic theory, like a simplifying assumption in physics—expert tasters with extensive experience who can rank all options might approach perfect rationality, but that is not the state of most people most of the time. The model resembles the endpoint of learning rather than its starting point. Textbook ‘rational actors’ were never what the field actually believed; they were just a convenient launching point.

12:14 Life and death probability questions should add to 100%—they don't
When asked ‘what is the probability you'll live to 75,’ people answer with a number like 90%. But when asked separately ‘what is the probability you'll die before 75,’ the answer will not be 10%—the two should sum to 100%, but they do not. Camerer's collaborator Eric Johnson attributes this to ‘default endorsement bias’: the question frames attention toward survival or death accordingly. Frame effects are not trivial—salad dressing labeled ‘10% fat’ sells differently from ‘90% fat-free’. Advertisers and political consultants have long understood this.

15:02 Chess masters guess numbers like everyone else in this game
In the guessing game where players choose 0–100 and the closest guess to two-thirds of the average wins, most people reason only one or two steps deep—‘others will guess 50, so I'll guess 33; or others will guess 33, so I'll guess 22’—and almost no one reasons all the way to zero. The New York Times ran this with 50,000 players; the data shows 33 appears far more often than 22, and deeper reasoning is nearly nonexistent. Surprisingly, professional chess players perform about the same as amateurs in this game—deep strategic thinking appears to be highly domain-specific and does not transfer across domains.

29:55 Audiences can't reverse-engineer ‘no reviews’ as a bad signal
From 600 major theatrical releases (2000–2009), roughly 10% are ‘cold opens’—studios don't send films to critics beforehand. These films later show the lowest aggregate critic scores, indicating studios knew they had lemons and held them back. But the cognitive hierarchy model predicts that some viewers will read ‘no reviews’ as neutral rather than bad, like Sherlock Holmes' dog that did not bark—most people won't reverse-engineer ‘why isn't anyone reviewing this?’. Because of this reasoning gap, cold-open films outperform their true quality by roughly 15% at the box office.

40:19 Neuroeconomics began with a silent room of economists
In 1997 Camerer and George Loewenstein organized a conference in Pittsburgh bringing together economists and neuroscientists to explore whether economic questions could be studied with neuroscience methods. Most economists stayed silent throughout—in the field, admitting ignorance carries low status. Notably, Peter Diamond, Al Roth, and Paul Romer were all in that room and later won the Nobel Prize, yet except for Romer's one paper on emotion, virtually none pursued this direction. Neuroeconomics actually advanced only when Caltech acquired an unused brain scanner and a few professors were willing to bet their tenure on it.

52:11 People who think one step deeper activate stronger mentalizing circuits
In the guessing game, players who reason forward—choosing 22 instead of 33—show stronger activity in brain regions responsible for ‘mentalizing,’ understanding others' thoughts: the right temporoparietal junction and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex. The test works by showing subjects the same photograph twice, once asking ‘what is this person doing’ and once asking ‘why is this person doing that’; the activation difference in the second version indexes mentalizing. Camerer acknowledges research here is sparse, but existing studies point the same direction: strategic depth and mentalizing circuitry use are linked.

1:00:29 Gym check-in intervals form a nearly perfect power law
Analyzing gym attendance data from roughly 20,000 people over 1,500 days, Camerer plotted visit intervals—many short gaps, many long gaps, no bell curve—and on a log-log graph it traces almost a perfect line (R²=0.97), a ‘burstiness’ that should be extremely rare in social science data. He later discovered mathematicians proved in 1954 that non-FIFO queuing, where ‘priority queue’ admits some people ahead of order, produces power-law distributions; such results appear mostly in physics journals. Their ‘Neural Autopilot’ model—habit-driven decision-making tracking only two values, the last choice and reward reliability—reproduces this effect with a slope of roughly -2.

1:20:23 Light can make rat brains misread foul tastes as rewards
The brain contains neurons encoding ‘reward prediction error’, discovered in 1997 by Schultz, Dayan, and Montague in rodents. Using optogenetics, Camerer's team amplified these neurons when a rat pressed a lever and drank salt water it hated, creating artificial ‘this was good’ signals in the brain—the rat kept pressing despite its facial expressions and behavior showing it disliked the taste. Camerer calls this ‘neural gaslighting’: the sensory system knows the truth, but the hijacked reward signal drowns it out.
